name: AI/Engagement 1 Internal REVIEWED
content:
# Workshop 1
 
 # Why Democratic Engagement?
 
 **Speakers:** [Beth Simone Noveck](https:/thegovlab.org/beth-simone-noveck.html) (Founder of InnovateUS and Chief AI Strategist, New Jersey) and [Danielle Allen](https:/danielleallen.scholars.harvard.edu) (Director of the Allen Lab for Democracy Renovation, Harvard Kennedy School)
 
 The speakers frame democracy as a "technology" whose core "spine" (participation → decision-making → implementation) is misaligned with the internet/AI era and outline general ways AI can help repair that spine if designed around real public-sector use cases.
 
 ## Topics Covered
 
 #### 
 
 ### (1) Democracy as a misaligned technology
 
 Allen argues we should think about democracy as a technology. The 18th-century "upgrade" combined popular participation with representation to scale self-government beyond city-states, but that design assumed slow, place-based information flow controlled through official channels. Geographic dispersal served as a natural barrier; representatives served as necessary information brokers. The internet eliminated these constraints without updating the institutional architecture—what Allen calls "a communications revolution without a matching democracy revolution."
 
 Noveck adds that the web gave us the ability to talk at scale, but we failed to invest equally in listening, synthesis, or connecting participation to decisions. We were "so giddy about the talking" that we didn't notice "when you give everybody a megaphone, nobody can hear anymore." The result: a proliferation of tools and experiments, but too many leading to "the dumpster fire of our democracy that is social media, not the promise of participatory democracy we hoped for."
 
 #### 
 
 ### (2) The spine of democracy and the importance of participation
 
 Allen's central metaphor: representative institutions form a "spine" with three vertebrae — (1) citizens participate and share information, expertise, and opinions; (2) decision-makers deliberate and choose; (3) institutions implement and enforce. "Our job now, heading into 2026, is to upgrade that spine by using technology to improve each vertebra and, crucially, connect them together." The real trick is hooking them up so participation feeds into decision-making, which feeds into implementation, creating a responsive feedback loop.
 
 Then Allen identifies three values participation delivers:
 
 - *Information power* – capturing grounded human experience that data alone misses ("not all of our knowledge is represented in data")
 - *Legitimacy* – decisions with participation are "slower but less brittle" because people feel ownership
 - *Freedom as counterweight* – protecting ordinary people's agency against concentrated power in executives, markets, or platforms
 
 ### (3) Technology and place
 
 Allen argues that 1990s tech-for-democracy efforts failed because they treated technology as a replacement for place-based organizing — "global, borderless networks" that made geography irrelevant. But democracy is fundamentally place-based (districts, wards, municipalities, counties). The current opportunity is technology *and* place: using AI to enhance local organizing, designing digital tools that complement analog civic infrastructure. [Bowling Green succeeded](https:/medium.com/jigsaw/how-one-of-the-fastest-growing-cities-in-kentucky-used-ai-to-plan-for-the-next-25-years-3b70c4fd1412) because [Pol.is](http:/pol.is) was embedded in intensive local work—80–100 listening partners, physical QR codes, trusted community messengers. "Civic infrastructure now must integrate the analog and the digital."
 
 ### (4) Why AI now
 
 Allen sees AI as "roughly akin to electricity: it's going to work its way through everything." Concrete capabilities include language access (removing barriers for LEP populations), document synthesis (cutting through "mountains of time" to master governance documents), and sense-making at scale (making thousands of inputs actionable).
 
 Noveck emphasizes that AI lowers costs enough to enable combinatorial democracy — using multiple engagement methods in sequence or parallel rather than "picking one off the menu." "We could do a deliberative dialogue with a representative sample AND ask experts on a particular topic. We can knit these things together." The promise: serving legitimacy goals (inclusion, voice) and decision-quality goals (information, actionability) simultaneously
 
 ## Some points for course design
 
 Across modules and cases, return to what’s broken in the participation → decision → implementation chain and how processes repaired or failed to repair those links.
 
 Position AI as solving concrete problems (language access, comment overload, etc.) rather than technology in search of an application. Allen: "Harvest the serious pain points and consider how AI tools address them."
 
 Practitioners are designers. Frame engagement as managing trade-offs and designing processes intentionally: inclusion vs. efficiency, breadth vs. depth, legitimacy vs. actionability. Help staff think like designers using principles.
 
 Human infrastructure is vital. In case studies, emphasize the interpersonal, political, local, and design work required to tap into engagement and make technology effective.
 
 Democracy practitioners often focus on legitimacy and inclusion; collective intelligence communities focus on problem-solving and information quality. The course should reflect both traditions.
 
 There is no way to “hack” reluctant power-holders, and some issues are not great occasions for engagement efforts. Look for crisis moments, innovators at the margins with bandwidth to experiment, proof points that spread from margins to the center.
 
 ## Audience notes
 
 Several participants frame AI as serving surveillance or corporate interests. The course must in some way address transparency, safeguards, data control, etc.
 
 Language access is a priority. Practitioners handling Limited English Proficiency (LEP) populations want to know specifically how AI can support translation and interpretation in elections and services.
 
 Performative engagement is a known problem. Some describe mayors or leaders as engaging performatively without acting on the results. This speaks directly to the course goal of making engagement more consequential (connecting the spine).
 
 There is a professional development gap for governance practitioners. Allen notes that the tech community routinely uses design principles, whereas the governance community often works from policy checklists rather than design principles. This limits the ability to adapt tools to the local context. The course should develop design thinking.
 
 ## Quotes
 
 ### Beth Simone Noveck (InnovateUS)
 
 "What the web gave us, and what we were so excited about, was the ability to talk, and we did not focus nearly enough on our ability to listen."
 
 "We were so excited at the time about 'my gosh, we could each express ourselves'... suddenly each of us had a blog... that megaphone thing was so exciting, and then suddenly when you give everybody a megaphone, nobody can hear anymore."
 
 "We've seen a tremendous proliferation of tools and experiments to engage people in deliberation, but too many of them have led to what Anne Applebaum calls 'the dumpster fire of our democracy' that is social media, not the promise of participatory democracy we hoped for."
 
 "It has been so costly to run meaningful engagements that we've always had to 'pick one off the menu.' AI gives us the chance to do more than that."
 
 "We don't have to choose just one method. We could do a deliberative dialogue with a representative sample AND ask experts on a particular topic. We can knit these things together... that's what I'm really excited about - not choosing winners among our favorite methods, but our ability to combine them."
 
 ### Danielle Allen (Allen Lab, Harvard Kennedy School)
 
 "The simple fact of the matter is that democracy itself is a technology."
 
 "Our representative institutions are, in some sense, the spine of our society, and we can think of that spine as consisting of three vertebrae: citizen participation, decision-makers deciding, and implementation."
 
 "Our job now, heading into 2026, is to upgrade that spine of representative institutions by using technology to improve citizen participation, decision-making, and implementation. The real trick is that you have to actually hook each of those vertebrae up together."
 
 "Democracy was designed for a much slower information flow, and for information flow that was fragmented by geographic dispersal... that condition has changed completely, and that destabilizes our existing institutions."
 
 "I think of AI as roughly akin to electricity: it is going to work its way through everything; the question is how we electrify our institutions in ways that actually help us."
 
 "Civic infrastructure now has to integrate the analog and the digital."
 
 "We've had a communications revolution but not a democracy revolution to match it. People can shout more easily than ever; that doesn't mean they're being heard."
 
 "What participation delivers: vastly improved information flows, legitimacy and sustainability, and freedom as a counterweight to other kinds of power."
 
 "Not all of our knowledge is represented in data. We would lose all of that if we only relied on data tools scraping the web. We need to activate the agency of real people as thinkers and contributors."
 
 ## Platforms/Tools/Cases Mentioned
 
 *Note: This session is primarily table-setting; detailed tool walkthroughs appear in later workshops. Tools mentioned here serve as examples of broader principles.*
 
 [**PopVox**](https:/popvox.com) — Legislative engagement platform. Caribbean legislature example shows how practitioners can actively correct AI bias: identified that LLMs lacked Caribbean English, worked to create new translation capacity tailored to community needs. Lesson: Practitioners can shape tools, too. Also, be aware of the local context/community you’re working with.
 
 [**Pol.is**](http:/pol.is) — Opinion-mapping platform using agree/disagree voting on user-generated statements. Used in Bowling Green, KY (with Jigsaw) for 25-year planning (8,000+ participants); VTaiwan for policy deliberation.
 
 [**Google Jigsaw Sensemaker**](https:/jigsaw-code.github.io/sensemaking-tools) — AI analysis layer on top of Pol.is-style input, used to categorize, synthesize without losing nuance, and find common ground (detailed in Workshop 9)
 
 [**Engaged California**](https:/engaged.ca.gov) — Wildfire crisis response using AI-assisted engagement (mentioned as an example of crisis-driven innovation)
 
 [**Hamburg DIPAS/DPAS**](https:/www.dipas.org) — Open-source urban planning platform with AI-supported analysis, now used in 9 cities (detailed in later workshop)
 
 [**GoVocal**](https:/www.govocal.com) — Belgian platform used in 500+ communities (mentioned as coming in later session)
 
 [**MIT Governance Lab**](https:/mitgovlab.org) **/** [**deliberation.io**](http:/deliberation.io) — Audio-based deliberation platform (deliberation.io) that transcribes and analyzes conversations for themes/consensus. [Piloted in Washington, DC for police policy input.](https:/octo.dc.gov/release/bowser-administration-announces-first-its-kind-ai-pilot-program-new-platform-mit-governance)
